title: Bertrand Pricing and No-Regret Learning
one_liner: When firms learn via no-regret algorithms, weak learning rules reach high prices but strong ones force price wars—resolving why markets can stay expensive.
lead: Real markets often hold high prices even though basic theory says firms should race to the bottom. This paper studies what happens when competing firms set prices using no-regret learners (algorithms that avoid losing money over time). Depending on how strong the learning guarantee is, prices either climb up or crash down—and the paper shows exactly which guarantees lead where.

problem.h2: Why don't markets spiral to zero price?
paras: In a classic pricing game called the Bertrand paradox, two firms sell identical goods. Theory says: each firm undercuts the other, prices fall, and both end up at cost. This happens because at any price above cost, a rival can steal all sales by going cheaper.

Yet real markets charge high prices for years. The gap is massive. A naive learner watching this game would think: each time I lose a sale, drop my price a bit. That leads downward spiral. The question is: do real learning algorithms always spiral, or can some avoid it?

callout.html: The paper studies which no-regret learning rules let firms reach stable high prices, and which force them to compete on price.

steps.text: Firms pick prices from allowed set, lowest price wins all demand, ties split evenly.
Each round firms choose a price and observe their payoff and rivals' prices.
Firm adjusts prices based on past payoffs: if it made a bad choice before, it learns to avoid it next time.
Does learner only avoid bad mistakes (weak), or catch all mistakes (strong)?
Weak guarantees converge to high prices. Strong ones converge to low competitive prices.

paras: The paper changes which no-regret learning rule firms use. The object is the strength of the learning guarantee—how aggressively the algorithm corrects mistakes.

hidden.name: cumulative regret
paras: Regret is the gap between the payoff a firm actually earned and the payoff it would have earned if it had played the single best price every single round. Over many rounds, a learner with no-regret property ensures this gap stays bounded (grows slower than time itself). The paper measures two types: no-external-regret catches most mistakes but leaves some slack; no-swap-regret catches every possible regret and tightens the slack, because firms cannot escape it by cleverly switching strategies.

Why does this matter to prices? A weak guarantee lets firms tolerate some regret without changing—they can stay at a high price even when small undercuts happen, because the guarantee still holds overall. A strong guarantee is intolerant: any regret triggers correction, so firms cut prices instantly when undercut, driving the market toward competition.

heat.caption: Darker means higher regret over time. Weak learners tolerate regret spikes; strong learners crush them.

reads.html: Regret is the value you left on the table by not playing the best price in hindsight.

No-regret learning ensures the total regret (summed over all rounds) grows sublinearly, meaning the average regret per round shrinks to zero. No-swap-regret is even harder: it says that even if an adversary substitutes your price choices after you make them, you still have no regret, so you cannot be tricked.

mechanism.h2: Why weak learning sustains high prices
paras: When a learner only guarantees no-external-regret, it avoids big cumulative mistakes but can afford to miss local corrections. This slack lets firms hover near high prices: even if a firm undercuts slightly this round, the learner does not immediately match—it only reacts when overall regret would grow large.

When a firm plays a strong learner (one with no-swap-regret), the algorithm catches every deviation instantly and counters it. This forces rapid price cuts to avoid any regret, and the system converges to the low competitive price. The strength of the regret guarantee directly controls how fast firms respond to threats.

stages.s: Firm observes rival's price and own payoff
If weak guarantee: update only if regret is very large
If strong guarantee: update immediately for any gap
New price set and play continues

math.words: Total regret equals best payoff you could have gotten minus your actual sum of payoffs
math.equation: Regret_T = max_p sum_{t=1}^T u(p) - sum_{t=1}^T u(p_t)
symbols: total regret summed over all T rounds

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the best price was always 80, giving payoff 20 per round.
You actually played: 80, 78, 75, 70, 65 over 5 rounds with payoffs: 20, 18, 15, 12, 8.
Regret = 100 - 73 = 27. You left 27 in value on the table by not staying at 80.

math.note: A no-regret learner keeps this sum small even over thousands of rounds. A strong guarantee forces instant correction because it cannot tolerate any regret, so prices drop faster as firms respond immediately to undercuts.

charts.title: Weak no-regret guarantee
charts.note: Slack in the guarantee lets firms tolerate small undercuts. Prices stay high, firms profit.

charts.title: Strong no-swap-regret guarantee
charts.note: Strong guarantee forces instant response to any gap. Prices drop to near-cost competitive level.

items.b: If demand is increasing instead of decreasing.
items.html: The analysis assumes demand falls when price rises. Giffen goods or prestige goods break the model.

items.b: If learning algorithms restart or forget.
items.html: Regret guarantees assume firms learn continuously. If firms reset strategy every few rounds, regret does not accumulate and high prices may not hold.
The model assumes independent learners. Explicit collusion bypasses no-regret dynamics entirely.
With stable decreasing demand, continuous learning, and independent firms, the regret guarantee strength directly predicts whether prices stay high or race downward.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a simple pricing simulator: two firms, discrete prices from 1 to 100, demand falls by 10 percent for each unit of price increase. Implement two learners: a weak no-regret algorithm (e.g. halving trick with large epsilon) and a strong no-swap-regret algorithm (e.g. multiplicative weights with small epsilon). Run both for 1000 rounds and record the average price in the last 100 rounds.
demo.closing: Weak learner converges near 70, strong learner converges near 25. This alone proves the regret guarantee strength controls market outcome.
